Example Travel Journal Destinations

A week of photographing invented lighthouses

The coast road between the made-up villages of Saltmere and Gullhaven passes five lighthouses in under sixty miles, and I spent a week trying to photograph each one at dawn, at dusk and in whatever weather the sea decided to send.

Saltmere Point is the easiest to reach. A short path runs from the car park to a bench facing the tower, and on a clear morning the light catches the red and white bands just as the lamp switches off for the day.

The second lighthouse, on the island of Little Skerrow, can only be reached at low tide across a causeway of slippery stones. I misjudged the timing on the first attempt and spent an anxious hour watching the water rise around my boots before deciding to come back the next day.

Further north the road climbs over the headland at Corrin Ness, where the lighthouse is now a holiday cottage. The owners were happy for me to set up a tripod in the garden, on the condition that I did not trample the herb bed, which I managed only about half of the time.

The last two towers, at Gullhaven harbour and on the far end of the breakwater, are close enough to photograph together. Fog rolled in on the final evening, and the only picture worth keeping shows two faint beams cutting through grey nothing.

Practical notes: the coast road is narrow, parking is limited at every site, and the tide tables matter more than any weather forecast. Bring a flask, spare batteries and a cloth for the lens, because sea spray gets everywhere.
